steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Food spoilage is caused by microorganisms (bacteria, yeasts, moulds) breaking down food.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Bacteria are the most common cause of food spoilage and food-borne illness.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Yeasts cause fermentation, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide — useful in bread-making but spoilage in other foods.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Moulds grow as visible fuzzy patches and can produce harmful mycotoxins.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What does FATTOM stand for? | Q: What is the danger zone temperature range for bacterial growth? | Q: Name three signs of food spoilage.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Food, Acidity, Temperature, Time, Oxygen, Moisture — the six conditions microorganisms need to grow. | 5°C to 63°C. Bacteria multiply fastest at around 37°C (body temperature). | Unpleasant smell, discolouration, slime, visible mould, gas bubbles, or off-taste (any three).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always refer to FATTOM when explaining how to prevent microbial growth — examiners look for this acronym. Distinguish clearly between spoilage (food becomes unpalatable) and food poisoning (food causes illness) — they are not the same. When asked about storage, always state the specific temperature: fridge at 0–5°C, freezer at −18°C or below. Use scientific vocabulary: say 'microorganisms' or 'pathogenic bacteria' rather than 'germs' or 'bugs'.
